title: Learning What Works by Experiencing What Doesn’t
author: Darlene S. Range
summary: Darlene Range, writing as a learning designer, compares two digital training experiences of her own: a hands-on Canvas course that built on her Blackboard experience, and a redundant online teaching certification that ignored what she already knew. She uses Merrill's First Principles, work on LMS adoption and Richard Mayer's multimedia learning theory to argue that support helpful to novices becomes wasted cognitive effort for experienced learners. She notes that the effective course let learners show competency and let experts have prerequisites waived. Her conclusion is a design rule, diagnose before designing, and a call to let experienced learners demonstrate what they know. The piece is a reflective personal case, but it ties its claims to named research.
points: Effective digital learning depends less on the technology than on whether the design recognizes what learners already know.
Learning an LMS by working inside it, with prior experience to build on, matched Merrill's principles of activation and application.
Mayer's point that novice supports can burden experienced learners explains why the repeated certification felt like wasted effort.
Letting learners demonstrate competency, such as submitting an existing course shell, avoids redundant instruction.
Diagnose before designing: the key design decision comes before the first screen is built.
quotes: What made the experience effective for me was that I was learning Canvas by actually using Canvas. I was not simply watching someone navigate the LMS or reading instructions about where different functions were located. I was navigating the environment, completing tasks, and gradually developing familiarity with the system.

Interestingly, research examining another institutional transition to Canvas found a similar pattern. Judge and Murray found that faculty valued structured training opportunities, but “jumping right in and learning by trial and error” was also one of the highest-ranked methods faculty reported using to learn Canvas (Judge & Murray, 2017). Their study also found that after faculty had taught with Canvas, they quickly developed enough competency that many no longer needed the same level of support. That reflects my own experience.

I experienced exactly that problem in another online professional development course. I was required by another institution to complete an online teaching certification even though I had recently completed comparable online teaching training at another college. The institution would not accept the previous training, so I worked my way through another lengthy course covering material that was already familiar to me.

The problem was not necessarily that the content was poorly designed. The problem was that the learning experience did not adequately account for my prior knowledge before determining how much instruction I needed. From the learner’s perspective, that distinction matters. A well-designed course can still become ineffective when it is delivered to someone who does not need that particular level of instruction.

Mayer explained that instructional support that benefits novice learners may not provide the same benefit to learners who already have substantial knowledge of the subject (Augusta University, 2024). This idea also connects with Clark and Mayer’s (2016) explanation of how learners integrate incoming information with knowledge already stored in long-term memory.

As a learning designer, that is the principle I want to carry forward. Before deciding how to teach something, I want to understand what learners already know and what they actually need to be able to do afterward. When possible, experienced learners should have opportunities to demonstrate competency rather than being forced through instruction designed for novices.

Both experiences ultimately taught me something useful. One taught me Canvas. The other taught me something about learning design. Sometimes the most important design decision happens before the first screen is ever built: diagnose before designing.
